title: Artemis II’s Mighty Rocket Disrupts GPS Signals, Reveals Hackaday Investigation】
body:
A NASA launch of the Artemis II mission this week generated a burst of electromagnetic interference strong enough to temporarily degrade Global Positioning System (GPS) signals across a wide swath of the United States, prompting aerospace engineers and telecommunications regulators to reevaluate the hidden side‑effects of high‑energy rocket thrust. While the spectacular visual and acoustic display of a launch is well understood, the incident underscores how the sheer power of modern launch vehicles can ripple through the fragile infrastructure that underpins everyday navigation, timing, and communications.

The Orion‑bound Space Launch System (SLS) lifted off from Kennedy Space Center at 9:47 a.m. EST, delivering a thrust of roughly 8.8 million pounds during its first stage burn. Within minutes of liftoff, GPS receivers in the eastern half of the country reported a spike in positioning errors, with some devices losing lock entirely for up to 30 seconds. The phenomenon, known as “RF interference,” occurs when the intense electromagnetic fields generated by the rocket’s engines and associated avionics couple into the radio spectrum used by satellite navigation. In this case, the interference was strong enough to be detected by civilian smartphones, automotive navigation systems, and even the timing circuits of power grid substations that rely on GPS for synchronization.

NASA’s Office of Safety and Mission Assurance confirmed that the SLS’s massive solid rocket boosters, which ignite with a sudden release of high‑energy plasma, are the primary source of the disturbance. The boosters produce a broadband electromagnetic pulse that can propagate upward and outward, interacting with the ionosphere and briefly overwhelming the relatively low‑power signals transmitted by GPS satellites. While the agency has long accounted for acoustic and mechanical shock effects on nearby structures, the electromagnetic dimension has been less rigorously modeled, especially for launch vehicles that exceed the thrust of previous rockets by a considerable margin.

Industry experts say the Artemis II incident is a wake‑up call for both launch providers and the broader satellite ecosystem. “We’ve always known rockets can affect radio communications, but the scale we’re seeing now is unprecedented,” said Dr. Elena Martínez, a senior researcher at the Space Weather Laboratory of the University of Colorado. “The SLS is essentially a moving source of intense radio frequency energy, and as we push toward more powerful, reusable launchers, the potential for widespread interference grows.” She added that the effect could be magnified in future missions that use even larger engines or employ multiple simultaneous launches from the same launch complex.

Regulatory bodies are already taking steps to mitigate such impacts. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) announced a review of its current guidelines for electromagnetic emissions from launch sites, aiming to develop stricter shielding and emission‑control standards. Meanwhile, the U.S. Department of Defense, which operates a fleet of GPS satellites, is exploring adaptive signal‑processing techniques that could allow receivers to filter out transient interference without compromising accuracy. Some commercial navigation providers are also considering the integration of alternative timing sources, such as terrestrial 5G networks, to provide redundancy during launch windows.

The Artemis II episode also highlights the interconnectedness of modern infrastructure. GPS is not merely a convenience for drivers; it is the backbone of financial transaction timestamps, airline flight plans, and critical national‑security operations. Even brief disruptions can cascade into larger systemic issues if not properly managed. As humanity prepares for an era of more frequent deep‑space missions, lunar habitats, and even crewed missions to Mars, ensuring that the tools enabling everyday life remain robust in the face of powerful rocket launches will be essential.

Looking ahead, engineers are already testing new mitigation strategies. One promising approach involves installing active electromagnetic shielding around launch pads, using arrays of conductive materials that can absorb and redirect stray radiation. Another line of research focuses on redesigning rocket avionics to emit lower‑frequency, less disruptive signals without sacrificing performance. If successful, these innovations could allow future launches to proceed without compromising the integrity of GPS and other critical services, paving the way for a seamless integration of humanity’s renewed ambitions in space with the technology‑dependent world on the ground.
